title: Why Leaders Sometimes Escalate Their Commitment to a Bad Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note asks why leaders so often double down after realizing a decision was bad. It argues the usual explanations of stubbornness, bad information or sunk costs are rarely the main cause, and that personal responsibility is the most powerful driver. Drawing on Barry Staw's research from the 1970s, it notes that people who made the original decision escalate far more than people who inherited it, because admitting error threatens competence and self-image. Public championing of the decision and loyalty to the people whose interests depend on it raise the pressure further. The note then offers defenses that must be built before a decision starts to fail, namely rewarding decision quality over outcomes and separating those who champion a decision from those who evaluate it. It closes with the point that admitting a mistake early costs far less credibility than defending it too long.
points: Personal responsibility, not stubbornness or sunk cost, is presented as the strongest driver of escalation, since the decision's author feels their competence is on trial.
The more publicly a leader has championed a decision, the greater the fear of looking weak by reversing it.
Rewarding the quality of the decision process rather than the outcome lowers the odds that teams escalate.
Separating champions of a decision from its evaluators gives an independent read when the decision starts failing.
Escalation is hard to see from the inside, so the safeguards have to be in place before the decision goes wrong.
quotes: This escalation of commitment is rarely caused by stubbornness, tenacity, or bad information. And only occasionally is the escalation a result of sunk costs or a simple unwillingness to walk away from investments already made.

Decades of research, beginning with Barry Staw’s experiments in the 1970s, show that people who make the original decision are far more likely to escalate than people who inherit it. Admitting that the decision was wrong threatens a leader’s sense of competence and self-image, so the mind looks for reasons to stay the course.
The more the leader has publicly championed the decision, the greater their fear of looking weak if they reverse course.
For instance, research shows that rewarding the quality of the decision process rather than the outcome is an effective way to avoid this trap.
Separating the people who champion a decision from people who evaluate it also helps to avert escalation.
Escalation is hard to see from the inside. The leader who made the decision is the person least able to judge it.
Admitting a mistake early costs a leader far less credibility than defending it too long. The best leaders make bad calls, too.
